A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same discriminator-guided audio-video generation work, renamed MMDisCo in v2. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy-distribution experiments, audio-video benchmark evaluations, and loss, architecture-size, and training-duration analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, discriminator variants, computational measurements, and a human preference study.

M1.justification: The discriminator objective, denoising regularization, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. V2 adds transformer-based fusion and ViT/ViViT feature-extraction variants in Appendix A.8. It also introduces video-gradient scaling by 8 specifically for Auffusion/VideoCrafter2, an inference adaptation beyond simply testing another model pair.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same toy distributions, Landscape, AIST++, and VGGSound, retaining the same in-domain and out-of-domain generation tasks. The additional model configurations and human assessment of existing VGGSound outputs expand evaluation procedures, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V1's OOD comparisons use unguided AudioLDM/AnimateDiff as the baseline. V2 adds unguided Auffusion/VideoCrafter2 and four sequential generation pipelines combining AnimateDiff or VideoCrafter2 with SpecVQGAN or Diff-Foley, evaluated on both Landscape and VGGSound in Tables 3–4.

E3.justification: V2 adds base-model configurations and guidance settings, timing experiments using batch size 8 on one H100, and a preference study involving ten sample pairs, eight evaluators, and four questions. It also replaces the previously cited official AV-Align computation with a stated 96 ms onset-detection interval for eight-fps videos. Earlier AV-Align coverage is reduced; the retained datasets and principal training settings otherwise remain stable.

E4.justification: V2 adds real-data loss ablations distinguishing fidelity from alignment effects (A.6), feature-extraction and fusion architecture comparisons (A.8), computational profiling (A.9), and diagnosis of AV-Align measurement failures (A.10.1). The earlier toy-loss, channel-size, depth, and training-epoch analyses remain, although their AV-Align results are partly removed.

E5.justification: The five-seed mean and standard-deviation reporting for Figure 5 is retained. V2 additionally specifies 500 repeated timing measurements per configuration and reports their means and standard deviations in Table 11. This concerns a new experiment, not an increase in repetitions of the existing generation study.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, model-pair, ablation, timing, and preference results. For example, the new Auffusion/VideoCrafter2 VGGSound comparison reports FVD 831 without guidance and 704 with guidance. For the retained AudioLDM/AnimateDiff Landscape experiment, guided IB-TV changes from 0.297 to 0.303 and IB-TA from 0.060 to 0.061. VGGSound AV-Align values change from 0.387/0.390 to 0.320/0.330 under the revised measurement procedure, so these are not comparable performance declines. Several earlier AV-Align entries disappear.

T1.justification: The joint-score derivations, assumptions, and discriminator proofs in Equations 1–36 and Appendices A.1–A.2 are unchanged. Appendix A.10.1 adds limited mathematical reasoning about AV-Align's boundedness and how nonunique peak correspondence can produce values exceeding one, beyond merely restating its standard formula.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: lightweight, model-agnostic discriminator guidance with denoising regularization improves joint generation while using frozen base models. The explicit statement that optimization requires no backpropagation through base models clarifies the existing black-box formulation rather than establishing a new contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation: it distinguishes the losses' alignment and fidelity roles, attributes advantages over sequential baselines to pretrained audio models' capacity and diversity, and discusses architecture-dependent performance. It also qualifies the timing comparator as a lower-bound training-cost estimate, acknowledges inference overhead, and motivates temporally misaligned negative pairs as future work.

D1.justification: V2 newly supplies a project-code link and documents guidance-scale selection, including its search grid. It adds transformer fusion layouts, positional embeddings, four-layer encoders, xFormers usage, and training details for the architecture variants, alongside hardware and procedures for the new timing and human evaluations. These substantially extend reproducibility information beyond v1's existing hyperparameter tables.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds a substantive comparison with Kim et al.'s discriminator guidance, distinguishing multimodal integration from single-modality refinement. References also expand to the added baselines, base models, and transformer designs, while several implementation references disappear. The broader positioning relative to MM-Diffusion, CoDi, classifier guidance, and DLSM remains intact.

P1.justification: V2 introduces the MMDisCo name, sentence-level copyediting, author-year citations, acknowledgments, a contents page, and additional appendix subsections. Existing sections and arguments largely retain their sequence and wording; the structural changes mainly accommodate added experiments rather than comprehensively reorganizing the narrative.

P2.justification: The OOD table is split into expanded dataset-specific tables, and new tables present loss ablations, architecture variants, timing, alignment, and human preferences. AV-Align columns are removed from retained benchmark and architecture tables, and Figure 5 is redrawn with three rather than four panels. The conference layout changes throughout, while the qualitative example figures are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens weaknesses in v1's validation: Tables 3–4 add competing generation pipelines and another base-model pair, Tables 7 and 10 test design choices on real data, and Tables 11–12 directly assess computational savings and overhead. These provide substantially stronger support for generality and efficiency than comparisons mainly against unguided models and parameter counts. Some temporal-alignment coverage is lost, and Table 14's percentages are not clearly reconciled with the stated human-response count. Those limitations constrain individual findings but do not outweigh the broader validation gains.
